# Transcaval Access for Large-Bore Structural Heart Interventions: A Clinical and Technical Review

## Introduction
Transcatheter structural heart interventions, particularly transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), have fundamentally changed the management of severe valvular heart disease [1]. While transfemoral (TF) access remains the gold standard owing to its low morbidity and rapid mobilization, severe peripheral arterial disease, heavy calcification, and tortuosity preclude TF access in a significant subset of patients [2]. Historically, alternative access routes such as transapical, transaortic, or subclavian/axillary approaches were utilized to bypass hostile iliofemoral anatomy [3]. However, these alternative surgical methods are associated with increased post-operative pain, longer hospital stays, and elevated rates of pulmonary and bleeding complications [4]. To address these limitations, a novel percutaneous alternative—transcaval (retroperitoneal caval-aortic) access—was developed [5].

## The Biological and Physical Principle of Transcaval Access
The biological and physical principle of transcaval access was first demonstrated in preclinical animal models [6] and subsequently validated in patients [7]. The technique exploits a unique anatomical and physiological concept: crossing from the low-pressure inferior vena cava (IVC) into the high-pressure abdominal aorta to establish a temporary conduit [8]. Remarkably, if bleeding occurs at the puncture site, retroperitoneal space pressure remains higher than venous pressure, causing blood to shunt preferentially into the low-pressure IVC rather than extravasating into the retroperitoneal cavity [9]. This auto-decompression mechanism serves as a physiological "safety valve" that protects against catastrophic retroperitoneal hematoma during sheath placement [10].

## Procedural Technique and Planning
Successful transcaval access requires meticulous preprocedural planning, which is heavily reliant on high-resolution contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) [11]. CT imaging is used to identify a "calcium-free window" on the infrarenal abdominal aortic wall directly adjacent to the IVC, ensuring the path avoids major lumbar arteries, the renal bifurcation, or thick calcified plaques [12]. 

During the procedure, femoral venous and arterial accesses are obtained, and a target snare is positioned in the abdominal aorta via an arterial catheter [13]. Simultaneously, from the venous side, a microcatheter is advanced into the IVC [14]. A dedicated guidewire is then energized with standard electrosurgical (electrocautery) energy to puncture across the retroperitoneal gap directly into the aortic snare [15]. Once captured and externalized, this wire establishes a secure aortocaval rail [16]. The tract is dilated with a balloon, allowing the introduction of a large-bore sheath (ranging from 14 to 24 French) from the IVC directly into the aorta to facilitate the structural intervention [17].

Upon completion of the primary structural procedure, the sheath is retracted to the aortocaval junction [18]. The channel is closed using an off-label nitinol cardiac occluder, typically an Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO), deployed across the aortic wall [19]. Complete closure of the tract and the absence of major retroperitoneal extravasation are confirmed via immediate abdominal aortography [20].

## Clinical Efficacy, Registries, and Alternative Access Comparisons
The safety and clinical efficacy of transcaval access have been thoroughly documented. The landmark, prospective, multi-center investigational device exemption (IDE) trial demonstrated a high rate of technical success (99%) and low 30-day mortality [21]. Subsequent registries and clinical cohorts have corroborated these findings, showing that transcaval access is associated with excellent procedural success and low rates of major vascular complications [22]. When compared directly with alternative surgical options like transapical or transaortic access, transcaval access shows significantly lower rates of acute kidney injury, shorter intensive care unit stays, and decreased 30-day mortality [23,24]. Furthermore, real-world registry data have confirmed a favorable learning curve, with procedural reproducibility and safety outcomes improving significantly after a center performs its first 10 to 15 cases [25,26].

## Complications, Pitfalls, and Mitigations
Despite its clinical utility, transcaval access is technically demanding and carries potential risks. The most feared complication is severe retroperitoneal hemorrhage resulting from incomplete occluder deployment, calcium interference, or vessel disruption [27]. While residual aortocaval shunts are common immediately post-procedure, the majority are hemodynamically insignificant and close spontaneously within several months, as confirmed by follow-up imaging [28,29].

## Expanding Indications and Future Perspectives
Initially developed for TAVR, the indications for transcaval access are rapidly expanding to other large-bore interventions, including mechanical circulatory support (MCS) insertion (e.g., Impella), endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), and thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) [30].

## Conclusion
Transcaval access is a vital, fully percutaneous alternative for large-bore structural heart interventions when transfemoral access is unfeasible. Guided by precise CT planning and a unique physiological safety profile, it offers superior outcomes compared to traditional surgical alternative accesses, significantly expanding the pool of patients who can safely undergo life-saving structural heart procedures.
